questions.prompt: Why can a negative-feedback loop whose loop gain has only ONE pole never become unstable?
options: Because a single pole has no gain
A single pole contributes at most \(-90^\circ\) of phase, so \(T\) can never reach \(-180^\circ\) (i.e. \(T=-1\))
Because a single pole makes the loop gain grow with frequency
Because single-pole loops have no feedback
questions.explanation: \(\angle\dfrac{T_0}{1+j\omega\tau}=-\tan^{-1}(\omega\tau)\to-90^\circ\) at most (reader Eq. 17.50 and Sec. 17.9.2). The feedback never turns positive, so there is always at least \(90^\circ\) of phase margin.

questions.prompt: A feedback system oscillates at a frequency \(\omega_x\) when
options: \(T(j\omega_x)=-1\): unity magnitude with \(-180^\circ\) phase, so the closed-loop gain \(G/(1+T)\) is infinite
\(T(j\omega_x)=+1\)
\(T(j\omega_x)=0\)
\(|T(j\omega_x)|\) is very large with \(0^\circ\) phase
questions.explanation:
With \(T=-1\), the denominator \(1+T\) vanishes (reader Sec. 17.9.3): a signal going around the loop comes back with the same size and inverted twice (the \(-180^\circ\) plus the subtraction), so it sustains itself without any input.
• \(T=+1\) gives \(1+T=2\), harmless in negative feedback.
• Large \(T\) at \(0^\circ\) is just strong, well-behaved negative feedback.

questions.prompt: At the frequency where \(|T|=1\), the loop-gain phase is \(-120^\circ\). What is the phase margin, in degrees?
questions.explanation: Phase margin \(=180^\circ+\angle T\) at the unity-loop-gain frequency \(=180^\circ-120^\circ=60^\circ\). The reader recommends at least \(60^\circ\) for a good design.

questions.prompt: A loop gain has \(T(jf)=\dfrac{1000}{(1+jf/1\ \mathrm{kHz})(1+jf/1\ \mathrm{MHz})}\). Find the frequency where \(|T|=1\) numerically and give the phase margin, in degrees.
questions.explanation:
The asymptotes say the crossover is near 1 MHz, right at the second pole, where the actual \(|T|\) is \(1/\sqrt2\) below the asymptote. Solving \(|T(jf)|=1\) gives \(f_c=786.2\ \mathrm{kHz}\).
\(\angle T(f_c)=-\tan^{-1}(f_c/1\ \mathrm{kHz})-\tan^{-1}(f_c/1\ \mathrm{MHz})=-128.1^\circ\), so PM \(=51.9^\circ\).
Using the asymptotic crossover (1 MHz) would give \(45^\circ\); the true answer is better because the crossover is lower.

questions.prompt: For the same loop gain (poles at 1 kHz and 1 MHz), what is \(\angle T\) at exactly 1 MHz, in degrees?
questions.explanation:
\(-\tan^{-1}(1000)-\tan^{-1}(1)=-89.94^\circ-45^\circ=-134.94^\circ\).
Two poles approach \(-180^\circ\) only asymptotically (reader Fig. 17.28); at the second pole you are \(45^\circ\) short of it.

questions.prompt: In a loop with a dominant pole and one non-dominant pole, where should the non-dominant pole be placed for a comfortable phase margin?
options: Exactly at the unity-loop-gain frequency, giving \(90^\circ\) margin
Below the dominant pole
Anywhere: non-dominant poles do not affect stability
Well above the unity-loop-gain frequency, so it adds little phase where \(|T|=1\) (at the crossover it would give only about \(45^\circ\))
questions.explanation:
At crossover the dominant pole already contributes \(\approx-90^\circ\). A second pole AT the crossover adds \(-45^\circ\) (PM \(\approx45^\circ\)); at \(\sim1.7\times\) the crossover it adds \(\approx-30^\circ\) (PM \(\approx60^\circ\)). So non-dominant poles belong well above the crossover (reader Sec. 17.9.2).
• A pole below the dominant one would make IT the dominant pole.

questions.prompt: An op-amp is stable as a gain-of-10 amplifier but oscillates when connected as a unity-gain follower. Why?
options: Because the follower has no feedback
Because the follower's gain of 1 means \(T=1\) at all frequencies
With \(f=1\) the loop gain \(T=Af\) is 10× larger, so the crossover moves up toward the non-dominant poles and the phase margin shrinks
Because lower closed-loop gain always gives MORE phase margin, so this can't happen
questions.explanation:
\(T=A(j\omega)f\): raising \(f\) from 0.1 to 1 lifts the whole \(|T|\) curve by 20 dB, so the unity crossing moves from \(\approx f_u/10\) to \(\approx f_u\), closer to the extra poles. The follower is the hardest case, which is why datasheets advertise 'unity-gain stable' op-amps.
Gotcha: low closed-loop gain means HIGH loop gain, and less margin.

questions.prompt: An op-amp has \(A(jf)=\dfrac{10^5}{(1+jf/10\ \mathrm{Hz})(1+jf/2\ \mathrm{MHz})}\) (\(f_u\approx1\ \mathrm{MHz}\)). Connected as a follower (\(f=1\)), what is the phase margin? Solve \(|T|=1\) numerically.
questions.explanation:
\(T=A\). Solving \(|A(jf)|=1\): \(f_c=910.2\ \mathrm{kHz}\) (a bit below 1 MHz because the second pole already bends the curve).
\(\angle T=-\tan^{-1}(f_c/10)-\tan^{-1}(f_c/2\ \mathrm{MHz})\approx-90^\circ-24.5^\circ\), so PM \(=65.5^\circ\).
With \(f=0.1\) the crossover drops to \(\approx100\ \mathrm{kHz}\) and PM \(\approx87^\circ\): same op-amp, very different margin.

questions.prompt: At the frequency where \(\angle T=-180^\circ\), a loop has \(|T|=0.3\). Is it stable?
options: No: any loop that reaches \(-180^\circ\) oscillates
Yes: the feedback is positive at that frequency, but with \(|T|<1\) the signal shrinks each trip around the loop (gain margin about 10.5 dB)
No: \(|T|=0.3\) is too small for feedback to work
It can't be determined without the DC gain
questions.explanation:
Oscillation needs \(T=-1\). With \(T=-0.3\), the closed-loop gain is \(G/(1-0.3)=1.43G\): a mild peak, not instability (reader Sec. 17.9.4: unstable if \(|T|>1\) at \(-180^\circ\)). The distance \(20\log(1/0.3)=10.5\ \mathrm{dB}\) is the gain margin.
Gotcha: reaching \(-180^\circ\) is not by itself fatal; it's the magnitude there that matters.

questions.prompt: Preview of capacitive loads. A follower's op-amp (\(A\approx f_u/jf\), \(f_u=1\ \mathrm{MHz}\)) has \(R_{out}=100\ \Omega\) and drives \(C_L=4.7\ \mathrm{nF}\). The load adds a pole at \(1/(2\pi R_{out}C_L)\). What is the phase margin? Solve \(|T|=1\) numerically.
questions.explanation:
Load pole: \(f_{p2}=\dfrac{1}{2\pi\cdot100\ \Omega\cdot4.7\ \mathrm{nF}}=0.339\ \mathrm{MHz}\). With \(T=\dfrac{f_u}{jf}\cdot\dfrac{1}{1+jf/f_{p2}}\), \(|T|=1\) at \(f_c=534.9\ \mathrm{kHz}\).
\(\angle T=-90^\circ-\tan^{-1}(f_c/f_{p2})\), so PM \(=32.3^\circ\): below the 60° target. Common-source stages with big capacitive loads face the same pole.

questions.prompt: Preview of compensation. A follower's loop gain is \(T=\dfrac{f_u}{jf}\cdot\dfrac{1}{1+jf/f_{p2}}\) with a non-dominant pole \(f_{p2}=10\ \mathrm{MHz}\). Dominant-pole compensation sets \(f_u\). Which \(f_u\) puts the crossover exactly at \(f_{p2}\) (phase margin \(45^\circ\)), in MHz?
questions.explanation:
At \(f=f_{p2}\): \(|T|=\dfrac{f_u}{f_{p2}}\cdot\dfrac{1}{\sqrt2}=1\Rightarrow f_u=\sqrt2\,f_{p2}=14.14\ \mathrm{MHz}\).
For 60° you would need \(f_u\) lower still. Designers lower \(f_u\) by enlarging the dominant capacitance, often with the Miller effect, which is coming soon.

questions.prompt: Preview of compensation. The follower driving \(C_L\) has too little phase margin. Using only stability ideas, which change helps?
options: Lower the op-amp's \(f_u\) (more dominant-pole compensation), so the crossover moves well below the load pole
Increase \(C_L\) further
Raise \(f_u\) so the loop is faster
Increase the feedback factor beyond 1
questions.explanation:
Phase margin improves when the crossover sits far below the non-dominant pole. Lowering \(f_u\) moves the crossover down. A larger \(C_L\) moves the load pole DOWN (worse). Raising \(f_u\) pushes the crossover up into the pole (worse). \(f\) can't exceed 1 with a passive network.
Miller compensation is the classic way to lower \(f_u\) on-chip.
